verdict.root_cause: Undetermined. Every one of the four available dispatches was spent on the same question — the change log — for frontend, checkoutservice, cartservice and productcatalogservice, and all four returned empty (tr_0c087f159665, tr_b35840897490, tr_c82e27e94094, tr_f078e2a13eef). That is a real but narrow result: it excludes a deploy, config push or flag flip on any of those four services in the 10 minutes before and 5 minutes after the 10:15:30 onset. It says nothing about what the services are actually doing wrong. No metrics, logs, traces, resource counters or dependency-health signals were examined at all, and the change window itself covered only 15 of the requested 90 minutes, leaving roughly 08:45–10:05 unexamined on all four services (tr_0c087f159665, tr_b35840897490, tr_c82e27e94094, tr_f078e2a13eef). Three of the seven services in the blast radius were never queried for anything, and triage flagged an unmeasured edge that remains unmeasured. With no observation of the failing mechanism — no evidence of saturation, of waiting on a slow dependency, of a wrong artifact, or of a wrong configuration value — assigning a fault class here would be invention, not inference.
verdict.reasoning: The only positive findings available are four absences of change records, each of high confidence but each scoped to a 15-minute window. Absence of a change near onset is evidence against a same-service self-inflicted change on those four services — the specialists correctly ruled that out — but it is not evidence for any particular alternative. Distinguishing resource_exhaustion from dependency_latency from bad_deploy requires looking at what the service is doing now: saturation counters, call-path latency, running artifact identity. None of that was collected. The three retrieved past incidents span three different fault classes (dependency latency, wrong image, flag failure) and their detection signatures do not cleanly discriminate here: this incident paged frontend first with loadgenerator 15s behind and grew to 7 services, which partially resembles the cart-dependency-latency shape and partially the wrong-image shape, and resemblance of alert fan-out is not a mechanism. Because a change-log absence is also consistent with the change simply falling outside the queried 15 minutes, even the exclusion is bounded rather than absolute. No remediation is defensible: rollback and config_revert have no identified target, restart and scale have no observed saturation or hung-process signal to justify them.
open_questions: What is the actual failing mechanism? No metric, log, trace or resource-utilisation evidence was gathered on any service.
Did a change land on any of the four services between 08:45 and 10:05, the ~75 minutes of the requested lookback that went unexamined?
What are the other three services in the 7-service blast radius, and were any of them changed or degraded? They were never queried.
What is on the unmeasured edge triage flagged, and does the failure propagate across it?
Which service is the origin? Frontend alerted first, but first-to-alert is not first-to-fail; a downstream dependency of frontend could be the source.
Are error rates or latency the dominant symptom? That distinction alone would separate dependency_latency from bad_deploy or resource_exhaustion.
Is the running artifact on each service the expected version? Nothing verified deployed image or build identity independently of the change log.
